subject: Re: [stan-users] Chains mixing poorly when fitting power law

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Chains mixing poorly when fitting power law
parts:
[move hijacked thread to stan-dev]

For every real argument to a *function* in Stan, it
can either be a constant (data, transformed data, local
constant expression) or a parameter (parameter, transformed
parameter, local function of parameter).

The apparent exception is integrate_ode, but that's not
actually a function --- it's its own special syntax.

- Bob

> On Mar 11, 2016, at 5:05 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hmmm, if uniform(L,U) works when L and U are parameters, then it should work when they’re constants, too, no?
>
>> On Mar 11, 2016, at 4:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> I'd rather not remove basic distributions. What do we do if
>> users have
>>
>> y ~ uniform(L, U);
>>
>> where L and U are parameters?
>>
>> Or if they want to get normalization?
>>
>> How about creating a warning with every use of uniform_lpdf() [get
>> used to it] that explains that if the variate is a parameter (or function
>> thereof), it needs to be constrained, and if the arguments are constant,
>> you might as well eliminate it. If you want to create an issue and give
>> me the language for the warning, it should be no problem.
>>
>> http://mc-stan.org/issues/
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Mar 11, 2016, at 4:06 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>
>>> And just in general we don’t like these sorts of uniform priors. Soft constraints are better.
>>>
>>> To Bob: This is another example of why I think we should remove the uniform distribution from Stan.
>>>
>>>> On Mar 11, 2016, at 7:58 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> On Friday, March 11, 2016 at 7:41:53 AM UTC-5, Ulf Mertens wrote:
>>>> I fit a power law to my data (y = a * x^b). The resulting chain (especially from cmdstan doesn't look good, see attached csv file that contains the posterior dists extracted from the output file of cmdstan (columns sdPow, aPow and bPow).
>>>>
>>>> When using rstan, there are less such areas where no sampling takes place, but still not the best mixing (a small part of the posterior is a flat line (see traceplot)
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> My .stan file (pow.stan):
>>>>
>>>> data {
>>>> int<lower=0> N;
>>>> vector[N] x;
>>>> vector[N] y;
>>>> }
>>>> parameters {
>>>> real a;
>>>> real b;
>>>>
>>>> a and b need <lower=..., upper=...> to match their priors. this by itself would be enough to kill sampling.
>>>>
>>>> real<lower=0> sigma;
>>>> }
>>>> model {
>>>> real mu;
>>>>
>>>> a ~ uniform(0, 200);
>>>> b ~ uniform(0, 2);
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> for (i in 1:N)
>>>> {
>>>> mu <- a * x[i]^b;
>>>> y[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>>>> }
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> The data:
>>>> x <- c(80,1,16,44,24,80,1)
>>>> y <- c(1000,10,140,450,250,1000,10)
>>>> N <- 7
>>>>
>>>> dat <- list(N = length(x), y = y,x = x)
>>>>
>>>> fit2 <- stan(file = 'pow.stan', data = dat,
>>>> iter = 5000, chains = 1,warmup = 1000)
>>>>
>>>> traceplot(fit2)
>>>>
>>>>
